title: The roof of the world
hookLine: Buddhism reached Tibet from the seventh century; its path is called the diamond vehicle

cards: Thin air. Hard light. A wind that never quite stops.
On the high plateau of Tibet, barley grows, yaks graze, and the winters are long.
Up here, over many centuries, a whole civilization organized itself around the Buddha's teaching: monasteries the size of towns, chants that rumble in the chest, colors everywhere.
For two weeks this path walked with the elders. Now it climbs. Today: the roof of the world, and the name of its path.

teach.h: KINGS, PRINCESSES, AN IMAGE IN LHASA.
teach.b: Buddhism reached Tibet in waves. Tibetan tradition says the seventh-century king Songtsen Gampo married princesses from Nepal and China, and each brought an image of the Buddha to Lhasa.
Later, King Trisong Detsen invited two teachers from India: the scholar Shantarakshita and the master Padmasambhava, whom Tibetans call Guru Rinpoche, the precious teacher.
Stories say Padmasambhava tamed the spirits of the land, and together they founded Samye, which tradition remembers as Tibet's first monastery.
More teachers followed over the centuries, carrying texts across the Himalayas to be translated with great care. The path they built is the Vajrayana. Yana means vehicle.
Vajra is harder to pin down, and that's the point. In old India it was the thunderbolt of the god Indra. In Buddhism it became the diamond: nothing can break it, and it cuts through everything.

teach.h: DORJE AND BELL — METHOD AND WISDOM.
teach.b: In ritual, a teacher holds a small metal dorje in the right hand and a bell in the left: method and wisdom, together.

The diamond vehicle keeps the Mahayana heart, the wish to wake up for all beings, and adds its own tools: mantras, visualizations, rituals, and a close bond with a teacher. You'll meet each of them over these two weeks.
Today it's practiced in Tibet and among Tibetans in exile, in Bhutan, Mongolia, the Himalayan regions of Nepal and India, and beyond.
Like the elders' way, it's learned here on its own terms, beside the others, never above or below them. The diamond vehicle.

how: Vajrayana Buddhism is practiced in Tibet, Bhutan, Mongolia, the Himalayan regions of Nepal and India, and in Tibetan communities worldwide; practitioners combine Mahayana teaching with mantra, visualization and ritual under the guidance of a teacher.

o: invite teachers from India to come and build.
forbid the old spirits of the land.

practice: Picture the high plateau: thin, cold air on your face, a sky so blue it's almost dark, a white monastery far off on a ridge.
Let the breath go slow, the way nobody hurries up a hill at that height, and feel how small and steady it is inside all that space. When the mind wanders, come back to the wide sky.

wordCard.voice: Vajrayana. The diamond vehicle: the Buddhism of Tibet and the Himalayas, named for what cannot be broken and cuts through.

orig.note: Sanskrit vajrayāna: vajra (diamond, thunderbolt) + yāna (vehicle). Tibetan: dorje thekpa.

carryVoice: Your line: the diamond vehicle. Steady as a diamond, sharp enough to cut. Day three hundred five, and the climb begins.
